lecture11.title: Masses and Springs · Theory and Prediction

sections.title: Masses and Springs · Theory and Prediction
One mass, two directions
teaching: An **oscillation** is repeated motion around an **equilibrium position**, the position where the mass can rest. Moving the mass away from equilibrium makes the spring exert a **restoring force** toward that position. The moving mass continues through equilibrium because of its **inertia**. It then displaces the spring in the other direction, so the restoring force reverses and brings it back again. The return force and the mass's tendency to keep moving together produce the repeated motion.

In **longitudinal motion**, the mass moves along the spring. Moving away from its resting position stretches or compresses the spring. The spring's restoring force opposes that displacement, so stretching and compression are followed by motion back toward equilibrium.

In **transverse motion**, the mass moves across the spring line. The outer ends stay fixed while the middle moves above and below its resting line. The segments are already under tension. When the mass moves off the line, their pulls have components that bring it back toward the line. The restoring action therefore works across the original spring line even though the segments pull along their own directions.

The two examples have the same **frequency**, meaning that they complete the same number of cycles in a given time. Their masses and total effective restoring stiffness are matched, even though their directions of movement differ. Direction alone therefore does not determine how fast the oscillation repeats. These ideal examples have no damping, so the oscillations continue rather than gradually dying away.

sections.title: Mass and stiffness change the rate
teaching: **Mass** and **restoring stiffness** affect different parts of an oscillation. Mass determines how difficult it is to change the object's motion. Restoring stiffness determines how strongly the system pulls the object back for a given displacement. Keeping one unchanged while changing the other lets their effects on **frequency** be separated.

A **larger mass oscillates more slowly** when restoring stiffness stays the same. The same restoring action has more inertia to overcome, so the mass takes longer to reverse and complete its motion. The larger blocks and circles therefore finish fewer cycles in the same time than their reference systems. Greater mass changes the rate even though the general back-and-forth pattern remains.

A **stiffer system oscillates faster** when mass stays the same. Displacing it produces a stronger return toward equilibrium, which changes the mass's motion more rapidly. The thicker-spring examples therefore complete more cycles in the same time. A stronger restoring action and a larger mass push the frequency in opposite directions.

These relationships apply to both longitudinal and transverse motion when stiffness means the **effective restoring stiffness in the direction of motion**. For the transverse systems, tension and the arrangement of the segments determine how strongly displacement produces a return toward the resting line. Increasing stiffness along a spring is not automatically the same change as increasing its restoring action across that line. Within each comparison, matching mass and effective restoring stiffness gives the two directions matching frequencies.

sections.title: Two masses have two normal modes
teaching: Connecting two masses allows their movements to affect one another through the middle connection. With equal masses, equal coupling elements and both outer ends fixed, the system has two **normal modes**. A normal mode is a coordinated pattern in which the masses keep a particular relationship to one another while the pattern oscillates at its own frequency.

In the **first mode**, the masses move together. When one is displaced in one direction, the other is displaced in that same direction, and they reverse together. This is the lower-frequency pattern. In the **second mode**, the masses oppose one another. When one is displaced one way, the other is displaced the other way. Their opposing movement disturbs the middle connection more strongly, adding to the restoring action and producing the higher frequency.

**Superposition** means adding the displacements contributed by the modes at each instant. Both modes can be present in the same pair of masses. Where their contributions point in the same direction, they add to the displacement. Where they point in opposite directions, they partly cancel. The resulting motion changes as the two modes move through their different cycles.

A mixture containing both modes still contains **two frequencies**. Its more complicated appearance does not turn it into a new single normal mode. The same coordinated relationships occur in the longitudinal and transverse versions when their effective couplings are matched. The higher mode is faster, but it is not simply twice the frequency of the lower one.

sections.title: Pop quiz
Three masses have three normal modes
teaching: Three equal moving masses connected between fixed ends have **three independent normal modes**. Each mode specifies how all three masses move in relation to one another. Adding a mass gives the system another independent coordinated pattern, rather than merely making the original pattern larger.

In the **lowest-frequency mode**, all three masses move in the same direction together. The middle mass moves farther from equilibrium than the outer two, whose displacements are equal. Moving together therefore describes their direction and timing, without requiring every mass to travel the same distance.

In the **middle-frequency mode**, the outer masses move in opposite directions while the middle mass stays at equilibrium. Their effects on the middle mass balance in this coordinated pattern. A part of a vibrating system can therefore remain still while other parts continue to oscillate.

In the **highest-frequency mode**, the two outer masses move together and the middle mass moves against them. The connections between the middle and outer masses are disturbed by this opposition, producing a faster pattern. The three mode frequencies are distinct, but they are not simply the first, second and third whole-number multiples of the lowest frequency.

All three modes can contribute to the same motion through **superposition**. Each mass's displacement is the sum of its contributions from the three patterns. The middle mass is stationary in the pure middle-frequency mode, but it moves when the other modes also contribute. A stationary location belongs to a particular mode, rather than being a permanent property of that physical mass in every possible motion.

sections.title: One more mass, one more mode
teaching: A chain has **one independent normal mode for each moving mass** in the direction being considered. The rows extend from one mass to six masses, with a matching number of modes in each row. A smaller chain has fewer independent ways for its masses to move together, so the empty spaces beside those rows do not represent missing examples.

Within a row, the masses and coupling elements stay the same and both ends stay fixed. The lowest mode has all the masses moving together. Higher modes introduce more **reversals in the spatial pattern**, dividing the chain into regions whose displacements point in opposite directions. Following a single mode over time shows those regions reversing together while retaining their relationship.

More reversals within the same chain are associated with a **higher vibration frequency**. Neighboring parts increasingly oppose one another, engaging the couplings in a stronger restoring pattern. The comparison concerns different coordinated motions of the same physical system, rather than different masses or springs being substituted between columns.

The **number of modes** and the **spacing of their frequencies** are separate properties. Having several independent modes does not require their frequencies to be whole-number multiples of the lowest one. These discrete mass chains generally do not form an integer harmonic series. Their displayed maximum displacements are matched to make the patterns comparable, and the colors distinguish mode numbers rather than individual masses.

sections.title: A fixed–fixed string combines harmonics
teaching: A string fixed at both ends must have **zero displacement at both endpoints**. These stationary points are **nodes**. The simplest standing pattern fits one half-wave between them, with the middle moving back and forth while the ends stay still. More complex patterns fit additional half-waves into the same length while still satisfying the two fixed boundaries.

The lowest mode has the **fundamental frequency**. The higher examples are **consecutive harmonics**, so their frequencies are whole-number multiples of that fundamental and include both odd and even multiples. Fitting more half-waves into the same string produces a shorter spatial pattern and a faster oscillation. The animation slows all the motions by the same factor so their different rates can be seen without changing these relationships.

Several modes can be present in **one string at the same time**. The combined shape adds their displacements at each position and instant. It can look much more complicated than any individual mode because contributions reinforce or oppose one another differently along the string and as time passes.

A **spectrum** separates the frequencies present in the motion measured at the marked pickup point. Frequency in hertz increases along the horizontal axis, and amplitude increases up the vertical axis. The five peaks correspond to the five harmonic components of the mixture. Their equal heights come from the chosen modal amplitudes at that particular measurement point. Equal peak heights are a feature of this constructed example, rather than a rule that every vibrating string produces.

sections.title: A membrane combines spatial modes
teaching: A **membrane** can form vibration patterns across a surface rather than only along a string. All four edges of this rectangular membrane stay fixed while its interior moves above and below the resting surface. A mode can divide the surface along either of its two directions, so its shape requires more information than a single count along a line.

The two numbers in a **mode label** count the half-wave regions in the two surface directions. The **(1,1)** pattern has one broad moving region. The **(2,1)** and **(1,2)** patterns each divide the surface into two regions, but along different directions. The **(2,2)** pattern divides it in both directions, and **(3,1)** divides it into three along the first direction. Adjacent regions in these divided patterns move to opposite sides of the resting surface, with stationary divisions between them.

The combined surface adds the five modal motions at each location. A marked **pickup point** identifies where that motion is measured. The spectrum places frequency in hertz along the horizontal axis and relative amplitude along the vertical axis. Its five equal-height peaks show the five components present at that point. The chosen modal amplitudes make those measured peaks equal, and the combined surface uses a smaller vertical display scale so its full motion fits in the panel.

The evenly spaced **harmonic frequencies** are deliberately assigned to this illustration. They are not the natural mode frequencies calculated for this rectangular membrane. The example demonstrates how different surface patterns can be combined and represented in a spectrum, while a natural membrane's modes do not automatically form an evenly spaced harmonic series.

sections.title: Theory makes a measurable prediction
teaching: A **scientific theory** describes how a system works precisely enough to predict what a measurement should show. **Differential equations** express how quantities change and how those changes depend on the system. Working out the behavior implied by those relationships turns the theory into a prediction that can be compared with the physical world.

The proposed model treats the **vocal folds as a vibrating membrane**. Its stated prediction is that a laryngeal vibration signal will have **equidistant harmonics**, meaning frequency peaks separated by equal intervals. The claim is about an observable pattern in the spectrum, rather than just a resemblance between the appearance of vocal-fold tissue and a membrane.

Testing that prediction would involve measuring **laryngeal vibration**, obtaining its spectrum and examining the spacing between the peaks. Regularly spaced peaks would agree with the stated prediction. A different pattern would raise a question about how well the proposed model describes the measured signal. The comparison links a claim about the physical system to evidence that can be examined.

The supplied material proposes this experiment without reporting a measured outcome. The membrane illustration uses assigned harmonic frequencies, so it does not independently establish that natural membrane modes always have that spacing. The scientific task is to compare the vocal-fold prediction with an actual vibration measurement.

sections.title: One fixed end and one free end
teaching: A **fixed end** and a **free end** impose different requirements on a string's vibration. The fixed bottom cannot move, so it is a **displacement node**. The free top can move and forms a **displacement antinode**, where the mode has its greatest displacement. A possible standing pattern has to satisfy both conditions together.

The simplest pattern fits a **quarter-wavelength** between the fixed and free ends. It begins at a stationary point and reaches a moving maximum at the other end. To fit a more complex pattern while preserving those same boundary conditions, the string must gain a full half-wave. That adds another node-to-antinode pair while keeping the bottom stationary and the top at an antinode.

The resulting patterns contain one, three, five and seven quarter-wavelengths. Their frequencies are the **odd harmonics**, consisting of the fundamental and its third, fifth and seventh multiples. An even number of quarter-wavelengths would leave a node at the top, violating the free-end condition. The missing even harmonics therefore follow from what the endpoints allow to move.

The spectrum has frequency in hertz along the horizontal axis and amplitude along the vertical axis. Its four equal-height peaks represent equal excitation of the four illustrated modes when the mixture is measured at the free end. The modes can all contribute there because the free end is an antinode in each pattern. The visible motion is slowed uniformly so the standing shapes and their different rates can be followed.

The fixed–fixed and fixed–free examples are **separately tuned** to share a fundamental frequency. Changing only a fixed endpoint to a free endpoint while keeping the string's length and wave speed unchanged would halve the fundamental. Matching the two examples therefore also requires changing length or wave speed.

sections.title: Masses and Springs in Speech Production
Dynamic systems in economic stabilization
teaching: An economy can undergo large changes over time, including boom-and-bust cycles. Woodford’s **Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium**, or DSGE, theory is the economic example of a theory about a changing system. The connection to physical systems is the question of how interactions produce fluctuations and how changing the system can reduce their size.

**Stabilization** means evening out peaks and troughs. Unemployment and inflation are drawn as jagged lines that become smoother where they are pressed together. The intended effect is to avoid harmful extremes such as high unemployment or runaway inflation. The illustration gives a qualitative goal for influencing a dynamic system rather than a numerical record of a particular economy.

sections.title: One mass, two directions
teaching: A displaced mass can keep moving back and forth because a spring and a mass contribute different parts of the behavior. The spring provides a **restoring force** toward equilibrium, the resting position. The mass has inertia, so its motion does not stop as soon as it reaches equilibrium. It passes through, deforms the spring in the other direction, and is then pulled back again. With no damping in the ideal model, this cycle continues. Frequency describes how often the complete cycle repeats.

In **longitudinal motion**, the mass moves along the spring. In transverse motion, it moves across the line connecting the supports. Both can oscillate because displacement produces a restoring effect in the direction of motion. The transverse system is already under tension, so pulling its middle away from the resting line creates a component of force back toward that line.

Changing the direction of motion does not by itself determine how quickly oscillation repeats. The two examples have matching masses and matching total effective restoring stiffness, so their rates match. The visible transverse excursion is enlarged to make it readable, while the model describes small movements around the tensioned resting state.

sections.title: Mass and stiffness change the rate
teaching: **Mass** affects how readily motion changes. With the same restoring stiffness, a heavier mass responds more slowly to the spring’s pull. It takes longer to complete a back-and-forth cycle, so its frequency falls. The larger-mass row therefore oscillates more slowly than the reference row in both directions of motion.

**Stiffness** affects how strongly the system pushes or pulls back for a displacement. With the same mass, a stiffer system produces a stronger restoring effect, changes the motion more quickly, and completes more cycles in the same time. Its frequency rises. Comparing one change at a time makes the cause clear: added mass slows oscillation, while added restoring stiffness speeds it up.

The relevant stiffness is the total restoring stiffness in the actual direction of motion. For the transverse system, that effect comes from tension and geometry. Its drawn thicker springs represent a stronger effective restoring effect; changing an axial spring constant alone while keeping the tension unchanged would not establish the same transverse change. These comparisons assume undamped motion.

sections.title: Two masses have two normal modes
teaching: Connecting two masses makes each mass’s movement affect the other through the coupling between them. A **normal mode** is a coordinated pattern in which the whole system repeats at one frequency. With two movable masses between fixed ends, there are two independent normal modes.

In the lower-frequency mode, the masses move together. Their separation changes little, so the coupling between them deforms relatively little. In the higher-frequency mode, they move in opposite directions. They approach each other and then separate, deforming the middle coupling more strongly. This stronger restoring involvement makes the opposing pattern repeat faster. The colored masses keep their identities as they move, and the dashed marks indicate equilibrium.

The same two coordinated patterns occur in the longitudinal and transverse versions when their effective couplings match. The directions look different, but the pattern of together versus opposing movement explains the difference in frequency in each case. Two modes do not imply that the faster mode is exactly twice the slower one; these are finite chains of discrete masses.

**Superposition** means adding the contributions of both modes at each instant. When their contributions point the same way at a mass, the resulting displacement is larger. When they point opposite ways, they partly cancel. The combined movement can look more complicated, but it still contains the two original frequencies. It is a mixture of the modes rather than an additional normal mode with a single new frequency.

sections.title: Three masses have three normal modes
teaching: Three movable masses between fixed ends have three independent **normal modes**. In the lowest-frequency pattern, all three move to the same side of equilibrium together. The middle mass travels farther than either outer mass, while the outer two move by equal amounts. This is the broadest coordinated pattern of the system.

In the next mode, the outer masses move in opposite directions and the middle mass stays at equilibrium. The middle is a **node**, a place with no displacement throughout that particular mode’s cycle. The couplings on its two sides balance so that it remains still while its neighbors move.

In the highest-frequency mode, the outer masses move together and the middle moves against them. This creates more reversals of movement along the chain and stronger relative deformation between neighbors. The pattern consequently oscillates faster. The longitudinal and transverse chains share these relationships when their effective properties match.

Adding all three mode contributions produces the combined motion. The middle mass now moves because the lowest and highest modes both contribute displacement there. Its stillness belongs specifically to the second mode; it is not permanently attached to a support. Each mode keeps its own frequency in the mixture, and the three finite-chain frequencies are not an exact sequence of integer harmonics.

sections.title: One more mass, one more mode
teaching: Each additional movable mass gives the connected chain one more independent way to move. A chain with one mass has one normal mode; two masses have two; the pattern continues through the six-mass chain, which has six. The number of modes counts independent coordinated patterns for motion in the displayed direction.

Within each chain, the lowest mode has the broadest pattern, with neighboring masses moving together. Successive modes introduce more reversals, so neighboring regions increasingly move against one another. More relative deformation brings a stronger restoring involvement and a higher vibration frequency. Colors distinguish mode number across the comparisons.

A one-mass chain has no second mode, and a two-mass chain has no third mode. This is why the arrangement has an empty triangular region. All available modes of each chain are represented. Their visible excursions are scaled for comparison, so a taller drawn movement is not a measure of a higher frequency.

Mode count and frequency spacing answer different questions. These chains have discrete masses, and their frequencies are generally not integer multiples of the lowest one. Counting more modes establishes more independent patterns without establishing the exact harmonic spacing of an ideal continuous string.

sections.title: A fixed–fixed string combines harmonics
teaching: An ideal continuous string fixed at both ends must remain still at both supports. Those endpoints are **nodes**. The simplest standing mode fits one half-wave between them, making one broad moving arch. The next fits two half-waves and has an additional node in the middle. Higher modes fit three, four, and five half-waves into the same length, with more internal nodes and more alternating regions of movement.

For the same string and wave speed, fitting more half-waves into the length makes the pattern repeat faster. These ideal modes form **harmonics**, with frequencies that are whole-number multiples of the lowest frequency. Both odd and even multiples occur because either number of half-waves can satisfy the two fixed ends. This exact spacing belongs to the ideal continuous-string model.

The combined string moves according to all five patterns at once. Every position has one resulting displacement made by adding the modes’ contributions there. Its changing outline can be complicated even though it contains a small set of orderly repeating components. The movement is uniformly slowed for viewing, so the frequency relationships remain the same.

A pickup at the marked point measures the motion at that location. The spectrum places frequency along the horizontal axis and amplitude vertically, separating that motion into five components. The five peaks have equal heights because the mode strengths were chosen to make their contributions equal at that pickup. Equal spectral peaks are a property of this particular excitation and measurement arrangement.

sections.title: Mass, stiffness, position, and frequency
teaching: Increasing a moving mass makes it harder to change the motion, so frequency falls when restoring stiffness stays the same. Increasing restoring stiffness gives a stronger return toward equilibrium, so frequency rises when mass stays the same. The direction of each effect follows from what changes in the balance between inertia and restoring force.

A small change in one part of a larger system is a **local perturbation**. Its effect depends on how that part participates in the mode being considered. Added mass has its strongest effect where the material makes a large back-and-forth excursion. An added mass at a node has little effect on that mode because it hardly participates in the movement.

Local **stretching or compression** concerns how neighbors move relative to one another. Neighbors can move a long distance together while keeping almost the same separation. That region has substantial motion but little local deformation. Elsewhere, neighboring regions move differently, so their separation changes strongly even near a location whose own excursion is small. Added stiffness matters most where this deformation is strong. In the ideal standing patterns, maxima of motion and maxima of deformation alternate along the system.

The spatial pattern and the boundary conditions must therefore be identified before predicting a change. A discrete chain has one independent mode per movable mass in the modeled direction. An ideal continuous string with two fixed ends has whole-number harmonics because whole numbers of half-waves fit. With one fixed and one free end, odd numbers of quarter-waves fit and produce odd-multiple resonances. These boundary rules do not turn every finite mass chain into an exact harmonic series.

sections.title: A fixed–fixed string combines harmonics
teaching: The different mode outlines are different contributions to the movement of one string. With both ends fixed, each pattern has endpoint nodes, while higher modes add internal nodes. Their allowed half-wave patterns give whole-number harmonics in this ideal continuous model.

When all five modes are active, their displacements add at each position and instant. A region can temporarily look almost flat because opposing contributions cancel, then become strongly displaced as their phases change. This changing combined shape still contains the five mode frequencies. Higher-frequency modes complete more cycles while the slower mode completes one.

Measuring only the marked point gives a changing displacement signal rather than the entire string shape. A **spectrum** reveals which frequencies contribute to that signal and how strongly each contributes at the measured location. Frequency increases horizontally, and peak height represents amplitude. Equal peaks here result from specially selected mode strengths at the chosen pickup; they do not require every point of the string to move equally in every mode.

sections.title: A local change affects two modes differently
teaching: The highlighted region is left of the string’s midpoint, and its role differs between the two modes. Mode 4 has a broad displaced region there. The material has a large excursion, while the nearby shape changes relatively little from one position to the next. Mode 5 passes near its resting line there, with a much stronger change between neighboring positions.

Added mass therefore has a strong slowing effect on mode 4. The added inertia is located where that mode moves substantially. Mode 5 has much less movement in the same region, so the same added mass has little effect on its frequency. The relevant motion is the excursion over a cycle, rather than whether a single frozen frame happens to catch a point at rest.

Added local stiffness affects the modes differently. Mode 4 has relatively little deformation in the marked region, so increasing stiffness there contributes little. Mode 5 strongly deforms that region, so the stronger restoring effect raises its frequency. If mass and stiffness both increase in that small region, the dominant outcomes are **mode 4 lower and mode 5 higher**. One physical change can affect two modes in opposite directions because the modes use that location differently.

sections.title: A membrane combines spatial modes
teaching: A membrane extends in two directions, so its **normal modes** can divide the surface in either direction. All edges remain fixed while the interior moves above and below the resting plane. The simplest pattern has one broad moving region. The next two divide the surface into two opposing regions along one direction or the other. Another divides it in both directions, making four regions, and the fifth has three moving regions along one direction. The two numbers in each mode label count the moving regions along the two surface directions.

The combined membrane has one resulting surface formed by adding the five motions at every location. Some contributions reinforce and others cancel as the phases change. The combined view uses a reduced vertical scale so that this sum fits, so its drawn height cannot be compared directly with the individual panels’ heights.

The marked pickup measures movement at one surface location. Its spectrum separates that movement into frequency components, with frequency horizontally and relative amplitude vertically. The illustration assigns evenly spaced harmonic frequencies and chooses strengths that produce equal peaks at this pickup. Those frequencies are an illustrative assignment rather than the rectangle’s natural mode frequencies. The example teaches how several spatial patterns can combine and appear in a spectrum; the harmonic spacing comes from the assigned frequencies.

sections.title: Theory makes a measurable prediction
teaching: A **theory** describes relationships clearly enough to say what should happen. For a changing physical system, differential equations can express how its quantities influence one another over time. Working out the model’s behavior produces a prediction that can be checked against measurement. The causal explanation and the predicted observation must stay connected.

Treating the vocal folds as a vibrating membrane motivates the proposed prediction about laryngeal vibration: the measured signal should contain regularly spaced **harmonic peaks**. The relevant observation is the spacing of peaks in a spectrum of the vibration signal. A test records the actual laryngeal vibration and examines its frequency components, then compares the measured spacing with the predicted pattern.

The illustrative membrane animation had its frequencies assigned. An independently recorded laryngeal signal supplies the separate evidence needed to test the prediction. The proposed experiment provides a testable question here; no measured outcome is supplied.

sections.title: One fixed end and one free end
teaching: A standing mode has to satisfy the conditions at both ends. At the fixed bottom, displacement stays zero, so the endpoint is a **node**. At the free top, the endpoint moves strongly and is an antinode. The simplest pattern connects those two different conditions with one quarter-wave.

Adding a half-wave preserves a node at one end and an antinode at the other. The allowed patterns therefore contain one, three, five, and seven quarter-waves. Their resonances are **odd multiples** of the lowest frequency. An even number of quarter-waves would end with the wrong kind of endpoint. The change from two fixed ends to one free end changes which patterns can fit.

The spectrum separates the allowed frequencies horizontally and shows their amplitudes vertically. Equal excitation gives equal peaks when measured at the free end, where each mode has strong motion. All motion is slowed uniformly for viewing, preserving the relative rates.

The fixed–fixed and fixed–free examples have been separately tuned to the same lowest frequency. With length and wave speed actually held constant, releasing one endpoint would lower the fundamental by half because the simplest allowed pattern becomes a quarter-wave rather than a half-wave. Matching their lowest frequencies therefore also requires retuning length or wave speed.

sections.title: Air in a fixed–free tube has modes
teaching: Air in the vocal tract can be modeled as small masses connected by spring-like couplings. The masses represent inertia, and the couplings represent air’s resistance to compression. The glottal end is treated as fixed in this simplified tube model, while the open lip end is free. Air elements move **longitudinally**, back and forth along the tube, rather than following a curved string outline.

The lowest coordinated pattern is the F1-like mode, and the next is the F2-like mode. **Formants** identify these resonances of the air system. The first mode has a broad movement pattern; the second has an additional reversal within the tube. For this uniform fixed–free reference, the second mode repeats three times as fast as the first, following the odd-multiple pattern.

Positions are measured from the glottis toward the lips. The /a/ region lies about one-third of the way along the tube, the /i/ region about two-thirds, and /u/ acts near the open lips. Each location must be examined in both modes because a region of strong movement for one pattern can be a region of strong compression for another. This makes constriction location relevant to the direction in which a formant changes.

sections.title: Vowel shape locates a constriction
teaching: Changing tongue and lip position changes the air passage through the vocal tract. A **constriction** is a region where that passage narrows. The MRI examples organize the tongue positions by height and by front–back location. “dean” is high and front, “Dan” is low and front, “dune” is high and back, “Don” is low and back, and “done” is central.

The narrowed region in the high-front “dean” example lies about two-thirds of the distance from the glottis toward the lips. The “dune” example has its labeled narrowing at the lips. The low-back “Don” example has a narrowing about one-third of the distance from the glottis. The central “done” reference is labeled as having no constriction.

These shapes connect articulation with the mechanical air model. A narrowing changes the local effective mass and springiness, and its acoustic effect depends on how that region moves or compresses in each mode. Knowing that a tongue position is high or back identifies its articulation, but the causal explanation of a formant shift also requires the constriction’s location within the mode pattern.

sections.title: Blank source page
Air in a fixed–free tube has modes
teaching: The two air-mode patterns occupy the same simplified tube, fixed at the glottal end and free at the lips. The upper pattern is F1-like and the lower is F2-like. They describe different coordinated resonances of the same air. The second mode has more internal changes in movement direction and repeats faster than the first; in the uniform reference, its frequency is three times as high.

To distinguish **motion from compression**, follow both an air element and its neighbors over time. If they all move together, the region travels while the spacing between elements changes little. If neighboring elements move differently, the gaps close and open strongly, producing compression and expansion. A point with little excursion can therefore sit in a region with substantial changing compression.

The one-third and two-thirds markers are measured from the glottis, with the lips at the free end. Comparing these same positions in both modes identifies which local mechanical effect will matter most. Where a mode moves strongly, extra effective mass strongly influences it. Where compression dominates, a change in springiness strongly influences it. The marked /a/, /i/, and /u/ regions supply three different comparisons of that relationship.

sections.title: /u/ loads the moving lip end
teaching: The /u/ constriction acts near the lips, the free end of the air model. Both the F1-like and F2-like modes have substantial back-and-forth movement there. **Free-end loading** represents increasing the effective mass involved in that movement. The larger drawn masses indicate a stronger inertia effect in the model, rather than heavier individual air molecules.

With restoring properties otherwise comparable, more effective mass responds more slowly and lowers a resonance. Because lip-end motion is important in both modes, the mass effect dominates both comparisons. The prediction is **F1 decreases and F2 decreases** relative to the uniform reference. The shared downward direction follows from the constriction acting at a place where both modes have strong motion.

sections.title: /i/ has opposite effects on F1 and F2
teaching: The /i/ constriction lies about two-thirds of the way from the glottis toward the lips. The same physical region participates differently in the first and second mode patterns. A constriction can increase local effective mass and springiness, but each mode is sensitive to those changes according to its own movement and deformation there.

For the first mode, the **mass effect** dominates. Air in that region participates strongly in the movement, so the greater effective inertia makes the cycle slower and F1 falls. For the second mode, the **springiness effect** dominates because the region undergoes strong local compression and expansion. A stronger restoring effect makes that cycle faster and F2 rises.

The result is lower F1 and higher F2 relative to the uniform reference. The local mass and stiffness changes do not have to cancel. Their effects are weighted by different local features of each mode, which is why one constriction can move the two resonances in opposite directions.

sections.title: /a/ reverses the two effects
teaching: The /a/ constriction lies about one-third of the way from the glottis toward the lips. Moving the narrowed region changes which part of each mode is most affected. The mass and stiffness rules remain the same, while the modes’ local participation changes.

In the first mode, local compression and **springiness** dominate at this location. Increasing the restoring stiffness makes the oscillation faster, so F1 rises. In the second mode, the local **mass effect** dominates. The greater effective inertia slows that mode, so F2 falls.

The result is higher F1 and lower F2 relative to the uniform reference. This reverses the /i/ pattern because the constriction is in a different region of the standing patterns. The explanation joins the physical location to the mode’s movement or compression there, then follows the appropriate mechanical change to its frequency consequence.

sections.title: Mass, stiffness, position, and frequency
teaching: The basic frequency directions come from two different physical roles. **Mass** supplies inertia, so increasing the moving mass slows the response when restoring stiffness is unchanged. **Stiffness** supplies a stronger restoring effect, so increasing it speeds the response when mass is unchanged. Greater inertia lowers frequency, while a stronger restoring effect raises it.

In a connected system, the location of a change matters because every mode has its own spatial pattern. A mass change matters most where that mode has large motion. A stiffness change matters most where the material stretches or compresses strongly. Neighbors moving together can produce much motion with little deformation, while different neighboring movements can produce strong deformation near a small-motion point. These are distinct ways a region can participate.

This local reasoning explains why a single constriction can move formants differently. At the lip-end /u/ region, the mass effect dominates the first two modes and both frequencies fall. At the two-thirds /i/ region, the first mode is slowed by mass while the second is sped by springiness. At the one-third /a/ region, those dominant effects reverse. The positions are measured from the glottis.

The number of independent modes and the harmonic pattern also depend on the modeled system. A finite chain has one mode per movable mass in the displayed direction, generally without exact integer spacing. An ideal continuous fixed–fixed string fits successive half-waves and has whole-number harmonics. An ideal fixed–free system fits odd numbers of quarter-waves and has odd-multiple resonances. Boundary conditions determine the patterns that can fit, while local mass and stiffness changes alter how those patterns oscillate.

sections.title: Compression and motion alternate in an air column
teaching: The moving air in the uniform tube labeled Schwa provides the reference. The other three rows isolate the first, second, and third modes at F1, F2, and F3. Blue circles represent air elements, and their motion is along the length of a tube closed at the left and open at the right. The rows let different coordinated patterns of the same air be examined separately.

As neighboring elements bunch together, the air is **compressed**. As they spread apart, it is rarefied. These changes create the spring-like restoring behavior of the air. The air also has inertia, so displaced regions continue moving and then reverse as the restoring effect acts. Compression and inertia together support repeated back-and-forth motion.

Large motion and large compression changes occur in different regions of a standing mode. Near a moving region, neighbors can travel together while their gaps change relatively little. Near a small-motion region, differing neighboring movements can strongly close and open the gaps. Following a whole cycle reveals this distinction more clearly than interpreting one frame’s particle positions as the complete pattern.

The closed end constrains displacement, while the open end permits strong movement. Higher modes add more alternating regions along the same tube, so the pattern of movement and compression changes with mode number. F1, F2, and F3 are separate resonances of one air system. A vowel can involve several frequency components rather than a single vibrating frequency or separate streams of air for each formant.
