sections.title: Masses and Springs in Speech Production
Mass, stiffness, position, and frequency
teaching: **Mass** and **stiffness** affect an oscillation in different ways. Mass gives a moving part inertia, so more mass makes it harder to speed up, slow down, and reverse. With the restoring stiffness unchanged, the cycle takes longer and **frequency decreases**. Greater stiffness produces a stronger restoring response to displacement. With the mass unchanged, the system returns and reverses more quickly, so **frequency increases**.

A system with several moving masses can organize their motion into several **normal modes**. A mode is a coordinated pattern in which the parts oscillate together at one frequency, although some parts can move in opposite directions. In the one-direction chains considered here, each additional mass adds another independent mode. Higher modes have more alternation in their spatial patterns.

The effect of a local change depends on **where it acts within a mode**. Extra mass matters strongly where a part makes a large excursion, because that mode must move the added load. Extra stiffness matters strongly where neighboring parts stretch or compress their connection. The places with greatest movement alternate with places of greatest stretching or compression in these ideal standing-wave patterns. A location that matters to one mode can have a different role in another.

**Boundary conditions** restrict which patterns fit. An ideal string fixed at both ends fits whole numbers of half-waves and has consecutive harmonics. An ideal uniform system fixed at one end and free at the other fits odd numbers of quarter-waves and has odd-multiple resonances. These simple harmonic relations belong to those ideal systems. A finite chain generally has frequencies that are not exact integer multiples, and changing the shape of a vocal tract changes its resonance pattern.

sections.title: One more mass, one more mode
teaching: A **normal mode** describes how the whole chain moves as one organized oscillation. With one moving mass between fixed ends, there is one such pattern. Two masses allow two patterns, and three masses allow three. The same relationship continues through the six-mass chain. Adding a mass adds another independent way for the system to move, rather than assigning that mass its own separate sound.

In the **lowest mode**, the moving masses are on the same side of their resting positions together. They pass through rest, move to the other side, and reverse together, although their excursions can differ. Higher modes split the chain into regions that move in opposite directions. Within a row, more reversals across the chain correspond to a faster oscillation.

The endpoints remain fixed while the connecting elements stretch and change direction with the masses. A mass at a stationary point of a particular mode can stay still while the rest of the system oscillates. The empty part of the atlas corresponds to patterns unavailable to the smaller chains. Every row has equal masses and equal effective coupling stiffness, so the comparisons concern coordinated motion rather than different materials.

The largest displayed excursions have been scaled to match, and colors identify **mode number**. A taller-looking moment does not establish a higher frequency. Frequency concerns how quickly a pattern completes its cycle. These discrete chains generally have noninteger frequency ratios, so counting their modes does not automatically produce the harmonic series of an ideal continuous string.

sections.title: Why fixed–fixed frequencies are integer multiples
teaching: Fixing both ends of a string forces them to remain at **displacement nodes**, where sideways movement is zero. The simplest allowed pattern bows out between those nodes and returns to them. That shape contains one **half-wavelength**. A half-wave connects one node to the next through a region of large movement.

The second mode fits two half-waves into the same length. Its two moving regions lie on opposite sides of rest and reverse together while the central node stays still. The next modes fit three, four, and five half-waves. Each additional packet introduces another moving region and another internal node, while both endpoints remain fixed.

Packing more half-waves into the same string makes each wavelength shorter. When wave speed stays the same, a shorter wavelength corresponds to a faster oscillation. That is why the illustrated frequencies are **whole-number multiples of the fundamental**, the lowest allowed frequency. Both odd and even multiples satisfy these endpoints.

The numbered packets identify portions of the standing-wave pattern. The first packet belongs to every illustrated mode, while each additional packet occurs only in modes with enough spatial divisions. These packets stay in their places along the string as the curves move up and down. They are not separate objects traveling from one end to the other.

sections.title: A fixed–fixed string combines harmonics
teaching: A string can contain several **modes at the same time**. At any position, its actual displacement is the sum of the contributions from those modes. Contributions pointing in the same direction reinforce one another, while contributions pointing in opposite directions partly cancel. Because the components oscillate at different rates, the combined string changes shape throughout the cycle.

The individual patterns all obey the same fixed endpoints. Their moving regions pass through rest and reverse, while the locations that are nodes of each component remain stationary in that component. Higher harmonics complete more cycles in the same time. The playback slows all of them by the same factor so that their relative rates remain meaningful.

The **spectrum** describes the movement measured at the marked point on the combined string. Frequency runs horizontally, and amplitude runs vertically. A peak’s position identifies how fast a component oscillates. Its height identifies how strongly that component contributes to the measurement. The five peaks are consecutive harmonics of the illustrated **100 Hz fundamental**.

Equal peak heights are arranged by the component amplitudes at that particular **pickup point**. They are not a general property of every vibrating string or every measurement location. One string can therefore have a complicated visible shape while its spectrum separates that motion into a few component frequencies. The shape at one moment and the frequencies present in the motion answer different questions.

sections.title: A membrane combines spatial modes
teaching: A **membrane** can organize its motion across two directions instead of only along a string. Its outside edges remain fixed while the interior moves above and below its resting surface. The simplest mode has one broad moving region. Other modes divide it into two regions in one direction or the other, four alternating regions across both directions, or three regions along one direction.

Adjacent regions separated by an internal stationary line move on opposite sides of rest. As the oscillation continues, the raised regions descend, pass through the resting surface, and become lowered regions. The divisions describe a stable spatial organization even though the membrane’s displacement keeps changing.

When several modes are present, their displacements **add at every position**. The combined surface can have bumps and dips that do not resemble any one component because different contributions reinforce or cancel locally. The combined panel uses a smaller vertical display scale, so its apparent height cannot be compared directly with the enlarged component panels.

The spectrum measures movement at a marked point, with frequency horizontally and relative amplitude vertically. The equal peaks were deliberately arranged for that pickup. The evenly spaced **illustrative frequencies were assigned**, rather than calculated as this membrane’s natural resonances. The demonstration explains how spatial modes combine and appear in a spectrum. It does not show that a rectangular membrane naturally has the same harmonic spacing as an ideal string.

sections.title: One fixed end and one free end
teaching: A **fixed–free string** must satisfy two different endpoint conditions. The bottom remains still at a displacement node. The free top can move through a large excursion and forms a displacement antinode. The simplest pattern therefore goes from no displacement at one end to maximum displacement at the other, fitting a **quarter-wavelength** into the string.

To create the next allowed pattern, another node and antinode can be inserted while preserving those endpoints. That adds two quarter-waves. The resulting sequence contains odd numbers of quarter-waves, giving **odd harmonics**. The second allowed mode is the third harmonic, because mode number counts the available patterns in order while harmonic number compares a frequency with the fundamental.

The separate curves repeatedly cross their resting positions and reverse while keeping the fixed bottom in place. The spectrum identifies the frequencies present in a mixture measured at the free end. Frequency is horizontal and amplitude vertical. The equal peaks reflect equal excitation in this setup, and the slow playback preserves the relative rates of the modes.

The fixed–fixed and fixed–free illustrations are **separately tuned** to the same displayed fundamental. If only the boundary changed while length and wave speed stayed the same, making one end free would halve the fundamental. Matching the fundamentals therefore also requires retuning length or wave speed. The matching labels do not mean the endpoint change has no effect.

sections.title: Why fixed–free frequencies are odd multiples
teaching: A **quarter-wave** connects a displacement node with an antinode. The fixed bottom requires a node, and the free top requires an antinode. One quarter-wave satisfies both conditions. Adding another pair of quarter-waves introduces a node–antinode alternation inside the string while still ending at the required free antinode.

The four patterns contain **one, three, five, and seven quarter-waves**. Each occupies the same total length, so the patterns with more packets have shorter wavelengths and higher frequencies. The second mode is the third harmonic, the third mode is the fifth harmonic, and the fourth mode is the seventh harmonic. The skipped even harmonics would end with the wrong kind of endpoint.

The numbered overlays identify how the packets accumulate within each mode. Every pattern contains the first packet. Only the higher patterns contain the additional packets, and only the highest illustrated mode contains the sixth and seventh. The counts describe the spatial shape, not how many cycles have already passed. During vibration, the moving parts reverse direction while those spatial divisions remain tied to the same locations.

sections.title: Count quarter-waves from the boundary conditions
teaching: The boundary conditions give a way to interpret an unfamiliar **standing-wave shape**. Start at the fixed bottom, which is a displacement node, and follow the curve toward the free top, which is an antinode. Every step from a node to an antinode or back spans a quarter-wave. The illustrated patterns therefore contain one, three, five, and seven such packets.

The pattern with more packets fits a shorter wavelength into the same length and oscillates faster when wave speed is unchanged. Counting the allowed patterns gives the **mode number**. Comparing their frequencies with the fundamental gives the **harmonic number**. The fourth allowed fixed–free mode is consequently the seventh harmonic. That conclusion follows from the endpoints and spatial divisions, without treating the label fourth mode as fourth harmonic.

sections.title: Air in a fixed–free tube has modes
teaching: Air in a simplified vocal tract has both **inertia** and a **restoring response to compression**. The chain represents those properties with moving masses and springs. The glottal side is constrained at the left, and the open lip end is free at the right. These different endpoint conditions organize the allowed air-column modes.

The particles move **longitudinally**, back and forth along the tract. When neighboring air elements approach each other, they compress the region between them. When they separate, that region rarefies. Their repeated reversal produces an acoustic oscillation. The moving particles are not tracing a sideways string shape or traveling steadily from the glottis to the lips.

The lowest air mode is labeled **F1-like**, and the next is **F2-like**. F1 and F2 identify resonances of the tract. In the illustrated uniform-tube reference, the second mode cycles three times as fast as the first, following the ideal fixed–free pattern. That simple relation can change when the tract becomes nonuniform.

The markers locate /a/ about one third of the way from the glottis, /i/ about two thirds along, and /u/ at the lips. They identify places within both modes. A perturbation’s effect depends on the motion and compression at that place in the particular mode being considered.

sections.title: Compression and motion alternate in an air column
teaching: **Air displacement** and **compression** describe different features of the same motion. Displacement concerns how far an air element moves from its usual position. Compression concerns how the spacing between neighboring elements changes. A region can undergo strong compression changes even when an element near its center moves very little.

The row labeled **Schwa** shows the moving uniform-tube reference. The three lower rows isolate the modes associated with F1, F2, and F3. In each row, air elements move along the tube, approach or separate from their neighbors, pass back through their usual positions, and reverse. The upper row also moves; it is not a static baseline.

The closed left end constrains displacement, while the open right end permits strong motion. Inside the tube, locations of strong displacement alternate with locations of strong compression changes. Higher modes contain more alternations along the same air column. The rows separate those patterns so that local behavior can be compared, although they all describe resonances of one air system.

sections.title: Vowel shape locates a constriction
teaching: **Vowel articulation** changes the shape of the air passage above the glottis. Tongue height describes whether the tongue is raised or lowered, while front and back describe where it is positioned along the mouth. These descriptions help identify where the passage narrows, which determines how the tract’s resonances are affected.

The examples **dean** and **dune** are both high vowels, but their shapes differ. Dean is high and front, with a constriction about two thirds of the way from the glottis toward the lips. Dune is high and back, with the marked constriction at the lips. The shared high classification therefore does not make their air passages or resonance patterns identical.

**Dan** is the low front example, while **Don** is the low back example. Don has a constriction marked about one third of the way from the glottis. The central example **done** is labeled No constriction and supplies the relatively unconstricted comparison. The source does not assign a numbered constriction position to Dan.

The distance is measured along the tract starting at the glottis. Moving a constriction changes which part of each standing-wave pattern is loaded. Articulatory categories describe the tongue and lips; the local balance of air movement and compression explains how that changed geometry affects F1 and F2.

sections.title: Why a constriction can raise one formant and lower another
teaching: A **constriction** changes how air moves and compresses within a region of the tract. In the lecture’s perturbation account, bunching air increases local density and its effective mass-like loading. Compressed air also resists further compression more strongly, giving a greater **stiffness** contribution. The tract images illustrate how changing tongue position reshapes that air passage.

The two contributions have opposite consequences for frequency. Where substantial air motion occurs, increased effective inertia makes the air harder to accelerate and reverse, tending to slow the oscillation. Where strong compression changes occur, increased restoring stiffness makes the return stronger, tending to speed the oscillation.

Those changes do not automatically cancel because **motion and compression are distributed differently along a mode**. A location with a large particle excursion can have relatively little change in neighboring spacing. A nearby location with little displacement can undergo strong compression and rarefaction. The same constriction therefore gives the mass and stiffness contributions different importance.

Each resonance has its own spatial pattern, so the balance must be evaluated separately for each one. A narrowing can act mainly on moving air for F1 and mainly on compression for F2, or the reverse. Opposite formant shifts follow from those different local roles, rather than from a change in the general mass–frequency or stiffness–frequency relationship.

sections.title: Compression and motion alternate in an air column
teaching: To identify a **motion-dominated region**, follow the excursion of an air element over time. A large back-and-forth excursion means that loading the moving air can strongly affect that mode. To identify a **compression-dominated region**, compare the changing gaps between neighbors. Large changes in those gaps reveal strong compression and rarefaction, even if a nearby element moves little.

The isolated F1, F2, and F3 patterns place their strongest movement and compression changes at different positions along the tube. A higher mode has more spatial alternation within the same length. A tract location therefore cannot be classified as motion-dominated for every resonance just because it has that role in one row.

The Schwa row supplies the moving uniform-tube reference, while the lower rows separate its resonant patterns. The closed end constrains displacement and the open end permits it. Comparing phases shows particles reversing along the tube rather than flowing through it continuously. That distinction allows the inertia and restoring-stiffness effects of a local change to be interpreted separately.

sections.title: Air in a fixed–free tube has modes
teaching: The **F1-like and F2-like modes** are two coordinated patterns of the same vocal-tract air column. The left end is constrained, and the right lip end is free. Both patterns allow strong motion near the free end, but the higher mode adds internal alternation in how neighboring regions move and compress.

The /a/, /i/, and /u/ markers refer to the same positions in both rows. The back marker is about one third of the distance from the glottis, the front marker about two thirds, and the lip marker is at the free end. Comparing a marker across the rows shows why a local constriction can have different effects on the two resonances.

Particle excursion identifies where the mode must move a substantial load. Changes in neighbor spacing identify where the compression-related restoring response matters. A useful qualitative prediction connects the **constriction location** with those local properties before assigning a direction to F1 or F2. The reference second mode runs three times as fast as the first in this ideal uniform-tube illustration; the perturbation reasoning concerns how changing the tract alters that reference.

sections.title: /u/ loads the moving lip end
teaching: The /u/ model treats the lip region as **free-end loading**. The enlarged masses near the right end represent a stronger mass-like contribution there. Both illustrated modes permit a large back-and-forth excursion near this free end, so both must move the loaded region during their oscillations.

Increasing the inertia of a region that moves strongly makes it harder to accelerate and reverse. When that contribution dominates, the system takes longer to complete a cycle. For the F1-like mode, local motion dominates and **F1 falls**. For the F2-like mode, local motion also dominates and **F2 falls**.

The shared downward prediction comes from the role of the lip region in both patterns. It does not follow merely from calling the vowel /u/ or noticing that a constriction exists. The source supplies a qualitative loading illustration and the direction of the predicted shifts, rather than numerical before-and-after measurements from a completed experiment.

sections.title: /i/ has opposite effects on F1 and F2
teaching: The /i/ constriction lies near the **front region**, about two thirds of the tract length from the glottis. It acts at the same physical location in both rows. What differs is the role of that region within each mode’s pattern of movement and compression.

For the lowest mode, **mass motion dominates** there. Air undergoes substantial movement, so increasing the effective inertia of that region slows the cycle. **F1 falls**. For the second mode, **springiness dominates** through local compression changes. A stronger restoring response makes that mode oscillate faster, so **F2 rises**.

The resulting low-F1, high-F2 pattern is possible because the same air passage participates differently in different resonances. A constriction can increase both mass-like and stiffness-like contributions without giving them equal influence on every mode. The direction follows from their local importance, rather than from assuming that one physical change must move every formant together.

These are **qualitative model predictions**. The moving particles and highlighted region support the causal account, while the source’s revealed reasoning states the two directions. The animation does not provide measured numerical shifts or an independent experimental confirmation of their size.

sections.title: /a/ reverses the two effects
teaching: The /a/ comparison places the constriction in the **back region**, about one third of the distance from the glottis. Moving the perturbation changes which part of each mode is affected, even though the principles governing mass and stiffness stay the same.

For the first mode, the back region is important to local compression and the restoring response. **Springiness dominates**, so increasing stiffness makes the oscillation faster and **F1 rises**. For the second mode, the same region participates strongly in air movement. **Mass motion dominates**, so increased effective inertia slows the oscillation and **F2 falls**.

This reverses the /i/ combination because the constriction is located in a different part of the standing-wave patterns. The explanation requires two linked comparisons: identify the affected tract position, then examine its movement and compression separately for each resonance. Neither vowel height alone nor the existence of a narrowing determines both formant directions.

The source establishes the direction of the **schematic prediction**, not a measured amount of change. The highlighted segments locate the perturbation and the particle motion illustrates the modes to which it applies.

sections.title: Compression and motion alternate in an air column
teaching: **Formants are resonances of the same air column**. F1, F2, and F3 correspond to different organized patterns available to that system, not separate streams of air. Their isolated rows show why one tract position can have a different acoustic role for each resonance.

Air elements move lengthwise, reverse around their usual positions, and create changing regions of compression and rarefaction. The Schwa row also moves and supplies the uniform-tube reference. The fixed left boundary restricts displacement, while the open right end allows strong movement. Higher modes add more internal alternation within that shared geometry.

Changing the tract at one position can therefore change several resonances by different amounts or in different directions. The relevant feature is how much each mode moves or compresses the air there. The physical cause is a change in that air system’s inertia and restoring behavior; the labels F1, F2, and F3 identify which resonances are being described.

sections.title: The source supplies harmonics and the filter shapes their heights
teaching: **Source–filter theory** separates two contributions to a voiced sound. The **glottal source** supplies a repeating vibration with harmonic frequency components. The **vocal tract filter** responds more strongly in some frequency regions than others because the air passage has resonances. Those resonant regions are its **formants**.

The source spectrum has frequency along the horizontal axis and amplitude along the vertical axis. Each narrow line is a **harmonic**, and the regular spacing reflects the source fundamental, **F0**. In this illustration the spacing is 100 Hz. The equally tall source lines simplify the comparison so that the filter’s effect can be isolated.

After the source passes through the tract, the same harmonic frequencies remain present, but their **relative amplitudes change**. Harmonics near a resonance become more prominent than those in less responsive regions. The broad pattern traced by their heights is the **spectral envelope**. The vowel pattern is carried by that envelope rather than by replacing all the harmonics with a single frequency.

The schwa comparison has four labeled resonant regions, F1 through F4, spread across the illustrated frequency range. The first produces the strongest low-frequency group, with further groups around the higher formants. These are schematic values for a relatively uniform tract, not fixed frequencies for every person. **F0 describes the source’s repetition rate, while F1 and the higher formants describe the tract’s resonances.** Their different labels reflect different physical causes.

sections.title: The /i/ filter keeps F1 low and F2 high
teaching: The /i/ pattern has a **low F1 and a high F2**. The first strong group of harmonics is near the low-frequency end of the spectrum, while the next resonant group is much farther to the right. A broad weak region separates them. Higher-frequency groups appear around F3 and F4.

The source retains the same harmonic spacing as the other vowel comparisons. This isolates the **vocal tract filter**. Changing the tract’s shape changes which harmonics it favors, so the line heights change while the source frequencies remain regularly spaced. The front constriction account explains the low first resonance and high second resonance through their different local balances of inertia and restoring stiffness.

The horizontal axis identifies frequency and the vertical axis identifies amplitude. A tall line at low frequency is strong, but it is still low in frequency. A shorter line farther to the right can have a higher frequency despite a smaller amplitude. Keeping those dimensions separate prevents a change in prominence from being mistaken for a change in pitch or harmonic spacing.

**Formants describe the envelope**, while the individual narrow lines are harmonics. The schematic /i/ values identify the filter used for this illustration, rather than universal values for every speaker. The vowel difference comes from reshaping the relative strengths of the source components, not from giving /i/ only two frequencies.

sections.title: The /a/ filter raises F1 and lowers F2
teaching: The /a/ pattern has a **higher F1 and a lower F2** than the /i/ comparison. The first strong spectral region moves upward in frequency, and the second moves downward. The two resonant regions are consequently closer together. Further groups of strengthened harmonics still occur around F3 and F4.

The source remains a regular harmonic series. The tract changes the **spectral envelope**, making different parts of that series prominent. Frequency still runs horizontally and amplitude vertically. A formant shift concerns where the broad region of strong response lies, while an amplitude difference concerns how tall an individual harmonic is.

A formant can lie **between two source harmonics**. In the illustrated first resonance, the neighboring harmonics are strengthened even though neither sits exactly at the labeled resonance frequency. The harmonics sample the filter’s response only at their own frequencies. A filter peak is therefore not required to coincide with a narrow source line.

The /a/ comparison supports the same source–filter distinction as the other vowels. A changed tract can shift the favored frequency regions without changing the source repetition rate. The labeled formants describe this schematic example; their role is to show the envelope’s pattern, rather than to prescribe one set of values for every production of the vowel.

sections.title: A spectrogram places successive spectra in time
teaching: A **spectrum** describes the relative strength of frequency components for one short moment. A **spectrogram** places such information across time, allowing a changing sound to be followed. The small spectra represent successive /i/ examples and then successive /a/ examples. Their different shapes describe how the distribution of sound across frequency changes.

The coordinate system changes when those spectra become a spectrogram. A spectrum places **frequency horizontally** and amplitude vertically. A spectrogram places **time horizontally** and frequency vertically. A low-frequency spectral peak becomes a mark low in the spectrogram. A high-frequency peak becomes a mark higher up. Moving to the right now means moving through time, rather than moving to a higher frequency.

**Darkness represents amplitude** in this grayscale display. A tall spectral peak becomes a dark mark at that frequency in the corresponding time slice. High amplitude is black, medium amplitude is gray, and low amplitude is white. The frequency position tells where the component lies, while darkness tells how strong it is. A darker band is not automatically a higher-frequency band.

During the illustrated change from /i/ toward /a/, the **first formant band rises** and the **second formant band falls**. They start farther apart and become closer together. Higher resonant bands remain above them with smaller changes. The changing band positions follow the tract’s changing resonances, while their darkness preserves the amplitude information that appeared as line heights in the individual spectra.

sections.title: Reflection prompt
Wide harmonic spacing makes formants harder to identify
teaching: A voiced source makes a set of **harmonics**, and those frequencies provide samples of the vocal tract’s response. With a low source fundamental, the harmonics lie close together. Many lines fall around a formant, allowing their relative heights to trace the rise and fall of a broad resonance region. The formant envelope is easier to recognize because it is described by several nearby samples.

Raising **F0** spreads the harmonics farther apart. Fewer lines now sample each resonant region, and a formant may lie between them. A strong isolated harmonic can be mistaken for the exact formant position, while an unsampled part of the filter remains difficult to infer from the sound’s narrow spectral lines. The resonance still exists even if there is no harmonic exactly at its peak.

The comparison holds the **vocal tract filter fixed** while presenting the same vowel at three source pitches. The top row shows progressively sparser harmonic samples of the same envelope. The lower row shows the corresponding spectrograms. With dense sampling, the resonance regions are easier to follow as formant bands. With wide spacing, the display can look more like separate harmonic traces, making the envelope less clear.

The toddler and soprano examples extend this problem to **high-pitched voices**. Their wider harmonic spacing can make formants harder to identify. A higher pitch does not by itself establish that the tract’s resonances have moved upward. F0 controls the spacing of the source samples, while formant frequencies concern the filter being sampled. Distinguishing those two changes is necessary before interpreting a high-pitch spectrum or spectrogram.

sections.title: Homework 4 lab reminder
Speech → Neural Networks
Five membrane modes combine into one motion
teaching: A **mode** is an organized way for the whole membrane to move. Its outside edges stay fixed, while regions inside them rise, pass through their resting position, and fall to the other side. Some modes have one broad moving region. Others divide the surface into several regions that move in opposite directions. The stationary lines between these regions are **nodes**. The regions on either side move while those lines stay in place.

The pairs of mode labels distinguish divisions along the two directions of the surface. A pattern divided across its width differs from one divided along its length, even though both belong to the same membrane. More divisions make the spatial pattern more complicated. The shape tells us where movement occurs; the frequency tells us how quickly that movement repeats.

When several modes occur together, the membrane does not choose one shape and discard the others. Their movements add at every location. Contributions in the same direction reinforce one another, while contributions in opposite directions partly cancel. This **superposition** makes the combined surface change shape as its component modes move through different phases.

A **spectrum** separates that complicated movement into its frequency components. The marked pickup observes one position on the membrane, so the strength it records depends on how much each mode moves there. The equal-height peaks were arranged by adjusting the component amplitudes at that pickup. They do not establish equal movement everywhere on the surface. The combined panel also uses a smaller display scale, so its drawn height cannot be compared directly with the height of an individual mode.

The five frequencies in this example were deliberately assigned as evenly spaced harmonics. That choice illustrates how components can combine; it does not describe the natural resonance spacing of every membrane. The playback is slowed so that the movement can be followed by eye. The frequency labels describe the intended oscillations, rather than the slow visible playback rate.

sections.title: A fixed end and a free end select odd harmonics
teaching: A **fixed end** cannot move sideways, so it must be a displacement node. A **free end** can move through a large excursion, so the permitted standing-wave patterns place a displacement antinode there. An antinode describes where the movement can be greatest over a cycle. It does not mean that the endpoint stays at its greatest displacement at every instant.

The simplest pattern connects the stationary bottom to the moving top without an internal node. More complicated patterns add stationary points and oppositely moving regions inside the same length. As each region reverses direction, the pattern keeps its nodes in the same places. A nearly straight-looking instant is a phase of the oscillation, rather than the disappearance of the mode.

The allowed frequencies are the **odd harmonics** of the fundamental. The second allowed mode oscillates at three times the fundamental, followed by five times and seven times. Mode number counts the patterns that are allowed. Harmonic number describes a frequency relative to the fundamental. The second mode is therefore the third harmonic, because a twice-as-fast pattern would fail the endpoint requirements.

The equal spectral peaks describe the particular mixture measured at the free end. All the displayed modes have antinodes there, and their excitation was chosen to give equal contributions at that location. The spectrum identifies their different rates even while the visible motion has been slowed.

The fixed–fixed and fixed–free demonstrations use separately tuned examples with the same labelled fundamental. To isolate the effect of changing a boundary, length and wave speed must stay the same. Under those conditions, changing from two fixed ends to one fixed and one free end lowers the fundamental to half its previous frequency. Matching frequency labels in separately adjusted demonstrations therefore do not show that the boundary has no effect.

sections.title: Quarter-wavelength packets explain the allowed modes
teaching: A **quarter-wavelength** is enough to connect a displacement node to an antinode. That makes it the simplest piece of a standing-wave pattern that can fit between a fixed end and a free end. The lowest mode fits one such piece into the available length.

Adding one more quarter-wave would finish at a node, which would make the far end behave like another fixed end. Adding two quarter-waves instead returns the pattern to an antinode. Each extra pair introduces another alternation inside the string while preserving the required endpoint behavior. The allowed patterns therefore contain one, three, five, and seven quarter-waves.

Fitting more of these pieces into the same length makes each wavelength shorter. With the wave speed unchanged, a shorter wavelength corresponds to a faster repetition. The odd frequency pattern follows from the **boundary conditions**, rather than from an arbitrary choice to omit the even harmonics.

The numbered pieces divide the shape of a standing wave. They are not objects that travel successively from one end to the other. The string moves back and forth while its nodes remain in place, and the more complicated modes fit more of those alternating regions into the same space.

sections.title: Air moves longitudinally in vocal-tract modes
teaching: Air has both **inertia** and **compressibility**. Inertia makes moving air resist a change in its motion. Compressibility allows a region of air to bunch together and then push back toward its usual spacing. A chain of masses and springs separates these two roles so that the air column can be understood through a simpler mechanical system.

The air elements move **longitudinally**, back and forth along the tube. When neighbors approach one another, the local air is compressed. When they separate, it is rarefied. The elements reverse around their usual positions, so the acoustic movement is different from a steady stream flowing out of the mouth.

The glottal end is constrained and the lip end is open in this simplified model. The lowest mode has a broad pattern, while the next mode fits an additional alternation into the same tract. In the ideal uniform-tube reference, the second mode repeats three times as fast as the first. That relationship belongs to this reference model, rather than establishing exact harmonic ratios for every discrete chain or every vowel shape.

The /a/, /i/, and /u/ markers identify a back region, a front region, and the lip end. Each position participates in both modes, but its movement and compression can differ between them. **F1 and F2** label the first two tract resonances. To predict what a narrowing does to them, the local role of the narrowed region must be examined separately in each mode.

sections.title: Track air motion separately from compression
teaching: An air element can move a long way while remaining almost the same distance from its neighbors. A different region can show little movement at its center while the neighbors crowd together and spread apart around it. **Displacement** describes the excursion of an element. **Compression** describes a change in the spacing and density of a group. These are distinct features of the same acoustic motion.

To follow displacement, track one circle through the cycle as it moves to one side, returns, and reverses. To follow compression, compare neighboring circles over time. A small gap at one instant is evidence of crowding then. Watching the gap widen and narrow reveals the changing compression, rather than just the direction in which the whole group is moving.

The closed end limits displacement, whereas the open end allows a larger excursion. In the lowest mode, the broad motion pattern places strong compression toward the constrained end. Higher modes introduce more regions that move differently from their neighbors, so strong movement and strong compression alternate more often along the tube.

The moving schwa reference and the separate **F1, F2, and F3** rows all represent air in the same kind of tract. The rows isolate different resonance patterns so that a single position can be compared across them. A narrowing at that position can affect the moving mass of one mode more strongly and the compressing air of another more strongly. That difference makes opposite formant shifts possible.

sections.title: Compare positions within an air mode
teaching: A position in an air column has to be understood through its movement over a cycle. Following one element reveals how far it travels from its resting position. Following the distances between neighbors reveals how strongly the local air compresses and expands. A still frame can show crowding, but the changing spacing explains the spring-like action that returns the air toward its usual state.

A region with a large excursion contributes strongly to the mode’s **inertia**. Increasing the effective mass there makes the moving part harder to accelerate and reverse, which tends to lower that resonance. A region with large compression changes contributes strongly to **restoring stiffness**. Strengthening that restoring effect tends to raise the resonance.

The same position can have a different balance in F1, F2, and F3 because the modes distribute motion and compression differently along the tube. A useful explanation therefore connects the marked location to the particular mode and then explains which effect dominates. The location alone does not determine an arrow without that spatial reasoning.

sections.title: Vowel positions change where the tract is narrowed
teaching: Vowels differ because the tongue and lips reshape the air passage above the glottis. **High and low** describe tongue height, while **front and back** describe its position along the mouth. These articulatory descriptions help locate a narrowing. They do not by themselves explain the change in a resonance; that explanation depends on how the narrowing affects moving and compressing air.

The vowel in dean is high and front, with the narrowing marked about two thirds of the way from the glottis toward the lips. The vowel in dune is high and back, with the highlighted narrowing at the lips. Both are described as high, yet they affect different positions along the air column. Their shared tongue-height category therefore does not require the same formant pattern.

The vowel in done is the central, relatively unconstricted reference. Dan supplies the low-front comparison, and Don supplies the low-back comparison. The narrowing marked for Don is about one third of the way from the glottis. That puts it farther back along the tract than the front narrowing associated with dean.

The starting point matters when interpreting these fractions. A position measured from the glottis follows the air path toward the lips. Moving the narrowing along that path places it in a different part of each mode’s pattern. **Articulation** specifies what shape changes, while the acoustic mode explains why that change affects F1 and F2 differently.

sections.title: A constriction changes inertia and restoring stiffness
teaching: A constriction changes more than the visible width of the tube. In the lecture’s mass-and-spring account, it changes both the effective **inertia** of the air and its **restoring stiffness**. Predicting a resonance shift means asking which of those changes matters more at the constriction’s location.

Inertia is the tendency of moving air to keep moving. If a mode requires substantial movement through the narrowed region, the added mass-like loading makes that movement harder to speed up and turn around. A full cycle takes longer when this effect dominates, so the resonance frequency falls. The important link is from local motion to greater effective inertia and then to slower oscillation.

Compression supplies the spring-like restoring action. Air that is pushed together resists further compression and pushes back toward its usual spacing. Where a mode strongly compresses and expands the narrowed region, a stronger restoring response brings the air back more quickly. The oscillation becomes faster when this stiffness effect dominates, so the resonance frequency rises.

The effects do not automatically cancel because the air does not move and compress equally at every position. Strong excursion and strong compression occur in different regions, and those regions change with the mode. The same constriction can therefore lower one resonance while raising another. Its acoustic effect depends on where it lies within each mode, rather than simply on the fact that the tract is narrower.

sections.title: Use both modes to interpret the same tract location
teaching: The first two air modes use the same tract but organize its movement differently. Both are constrained at the glottal end and allow strong movement at the open lip end. The second mode has an additional alternation inside the tube, so its local pattern of motion and compression differs from that of the first.

A narrowing occupies the same physical place for both modes. What changes between the rows is the role that place plays in the oscillation. Near the lips, both modes move air strongly. Farther inside, a region that moves substantially in one mode can undergo stronger compression changes in the other. This is why a single articulatory change can affect F1 and F2 in different directions.

The marked back, front, and lip positions make the comparison specific. At each position, first identify how much the local air moves and how much its spacing changes. Dominant inertia predicts a lower resonance, while dominant restoring stiffness predicts a higher one. The prediction follows from the local behavior, rather than from memorizing a single arrow for every constriction.

The three-times frequency relationship describes the ideal uniform reference. **F1 and F2 are tract resonances**, and changes in tract shape alter them. They are distinct from the harmonics supplied by vocal-fold repetition, whose spacing is controlled by the source fundamental.

sections.title: Lip loading lowers both F1 and F2 in the /u/ model
teaching: The **/u/ model** places the loading near the open lip end. Both of the first two modes have strong displacement there, so both rely on substantial movement of the affected air. The enlarged masses represent greater effective inertia at that location.

More inertia means that the moving air resists changes in its motion more strongly. It takes longer to accelerate and reverse when this mass-like effect dominates. Because a cycle takes longer, its repetition rate falls. This links the visible location of the loading to the direction of the acoustic change.

The same reasoning applies to both modes near the lips. The first resonance, **F1**, decreases, and the second resonance, **F2**, also decreases. Their shared direction comes from the fact that motion dominates for both at this location, rather than from a general rule that every narrowing lowers every resonance.

This is a qualitative prediction about the /u/ configuration. Its explanation is the chain from lip-region loading to stronger inertia and then to slower oscillation in both modes. The larger air elements still move back and forth; their size does not turn the acoustic oscillation into a steady outward airflow.

sections.title: A front constriction separates the effects on F1 and F2
teaching: The **/i/ model** narrows the front region, about two thirds of the way from the glottis toward the lips. The narrowing stays at that same position in both modes. Its different effects arise because the first and second modes use that region differently.

For the first mode, the affected region participates strongly in air movement. The constriction’s mass-like contribution therefore dominates. Greater effective inertia makes that moving air harder to turn around, lengthening the cycle and lowering **F1**.

For the second mode, the same region participates strongly in compression and expansion. The constriction strengthens a restoring effect that matters greatly there. The stronger return toward the usual spacing makes the cycle faster, so **F2** rises.

The result is a lower first formant and a higher second formant. The physical roles of mass and stiffness have stayed the same throughout. What differs is the spatial pattern of each mode, which changes the relative importance of the two effects at the front narrowing.

sections.title: A back constriction reverses the F1 and F2 pattern
teaching: The **/a/ model** moves the narrowing farther back, to about one third of the tract length from the glottis. The same back region is changed for both modes, but their motion and compression patterns give that region different roles.

In the first mode, strong local compression makes the restoring effect especially important. Increasing this spring-like response brings the air back more quickly after it is displaced from its usual spacing. The cycle becomes faster, so **F1 rises**.

In the second mode, the back region participates more strongly in movement. The constriction’s mass-like loading therefore matters more. Greater effective inertia makes reversal slower, lengthens the cycle, and causes **F2 to fall**.

This pattern reverses the front-constriction pattern because the narrowing has changed location within the modes. It does not reverse the roles of mass and stiffness. Stiffness still tends to speed an oscillation, while inertia tends to slow it. Connecting those effects to the local mode pattern explains the formant directions more reliably than treating vowel labels as isolated facts.

sections.title: Air motion and compression in the vocal-tract modes
teaching: An acoustic oscillation involves both the movement of air and changes in its local spacing. The circles move along the tube, reverse, and return through their usual positions. **Longitudinal motion** means that this displacement runs along the air passage, rather than sideways like a string’s visible movement.

A group of neighboring elements can move together through a large excursion without much change in the gaps between them. In another region, neighbors move by different amounts, so the gaps shrink and expand. The first situation emphasizes moving mass. The second emphasizes **compression and rarefaction**, which provide a spring-like restoring action.

The schwa row represents the moving reference air column, while the separate F1, F2, and F3 rows isolate its different resonance patterns. Higher modes fit more alternations into the same tract. As a result, the regions of strong movement and strong compression are arranged differently for each resonance.

A constriction affects the air at one location, but that location can have a different role in every mode. Added inertia matters most where air movement contributes strongly. Changed stiffness matters most where local spacing changes contribute strongly. Comparing those roles explains how a single tract shape can produce several resonances with different responses.

sections.title: The vocal-fold source sets harmonic spacing
teaching: The vibrating vocal-fold **source** supplies a repeating pattern of movement. Its fundamental frequency, **F0**, describes how often the pattern repeats. The source spectrum contains harmonics at successive multiples of that rate, so the fundamental also sets the spacing between neighboring harmonic components.

Effective inertia and restoring action help explain changes in the source rate. Heavier, looser folds reverse more slowly in this comparison. Lighter, tighter folds can repeat more quickly. The displayed examples move from a lower to a higher F0, and the harmonic stems become farther apart as the repetition rate increases.

The spectra use the same frequency window. A lower source rate places more harmonic components inside that window, while a higher rate leaves wider gaps and fewer components. This matters because the tract will favor some frequency regions over others. A dense set of harmonics supplies more points through which the shape of a resonance can be seen.

The membrane example also shows how several component movements combine into one changing motion. Its assigned harmonic spacing makes the combination easy to compare with a harmonic source. The surface patterns and the repetition rates remain different properties, and the deliberately chosen membrane frequencies do not establish that natural membrane resonances are equally spaced.

A voiced vowel therefore contains multiple frequency components. **F0** describes the source’s repetition and harmonic spacing. The tract resonances describe which regions of that multi-frequency sound become strong. A vowel is not a single pure frequency, and changing source pitch is different from changing the vowel-shaped filter.

sections.title: The vocal-tract filter favors nearby harmonics
teaching: The **vocal tract** reshapes the relative strengths of the source harmonics. Its air column resonates more strongly in some frequency regions than in others, so harmonics near those regions become prominent. Harmonics farther from a favored region are weaker in the simplified comparison. The tract acts as a **filter** because it changes the balance among components already supplied by the source.

A **formant** identifies one of these favored resonance regions. Changing the tongue or lips changes the air passage, which changes where its resonances lie. The closed–open tube provides the reference, and the central, lip-constricted, front-constricted, and back/open vowel configurations give different filter patterns.

The schwa example has separated lower and higher resonance regions. The /u/ example favors lower regions and also marks a third resonance. The front /i/ or /I/ configuration combines a low first resonance with a much higher second one. The /a/ example brings its first two targets close together. These comparisons describe the pattern of favored frequencies, rather than a different vocal-fold repetition rate for each vowel.

The marked target is a property of the filter, while a harmonic stem is a component of the source. A resonance can fall between two harmonics. In that case, the nearby components can be emphasized without creating a new source harmonic exactly at the target. Keeping those roles separate explains how the same harmonic source can acquire different vowel qualities.

sections.title: One filter can look different at different pitches
teaching: The vowel filter and the source repetition rate can be varied separately. Within a column, the tract shape and its **formant envelope** stay fixed. Moving between source rows changes F0 and therefore changes the spacing of the harmonics that pass through that same filter. Across a row, the source spacing stays the same while the vowel filter changes.

At a lower F0, closely spaced harmonics sample many positions within each favored frequency region. Their relative heights trace the envelope more densely, which makes the resonance pattern easier to recognize. At a higher F0, the wider gaps leave fewer samples. A target can lie between the available harmonics, so the tallest nearby stem can sit beside the target rather than directly on it.

This is especially important when two resonances are close. The /a/ filter marks two nearby targets, but sparse harmonic stems can make them look like one grouped region. Denser sampling gives more information about the envelope, although it does not guarantee two separately visible peaks in every case.

The stem positions identify actual harmonic frequencies, and their heights identify strength after filtering. The smooth envelope and target marks identify the filter. If the visible stems become sparse while the targets stay fixed, the evidence supports a change in **sampling**, rather than a change in tract resonance. A formant becoming difficult to estimate does not mean that the physical resonance vanished.

sections.title: Map spectra into a spectrogram
teaching: A **spectrum** describes the frequency components in a short slice of sound. Frequency runs from left to right, and the height of a component shows its amplitude. Comparing successive spectra reveals how the distribution of strength changes as speech continues.

A **spectrogram** puts those successive slices beside one another. Time advances horizontally, and frequency runs vertically. A component that lies farther right in a spectrum belongs higher in the spectrogram. Its amplitude is then represented by darkness instead of by the height of a stem: stronger components are black, intermediate components are gray, and weak components are white in this display.

These mappings separate two kinds of change. A band that moves upward is moving toward a higher frequency. A band that becomes darker at the same height is becoming stronger at that frequency. Confusing height with darkness would confuse a change in frequency with a change in amplitude.

During the **/i/ to /a/** transition, the lowest strong band rises while the next strong band falls. Those paths show the changing resonance pattern as the vocal-tract shape changes. The higher bands provide additional frequency information: one upper band shifts downward while a fainter band remains in the higher-frequency region. The continuous-looking paths come from adjacent time slices, rather than from a single spectrum containing a time axis.

The spectral stems and the spectrogram bands therefore describe related information using different visual arrangements. Following their frequency positions shows which regions are favored. Following their strengths shows how prominently those regions appear in the sound.

sections.title: Reflection prompt
Speech-complexity experiment prompt
Use formants as input to vowel recognition
teaching: **Formants** connect vocal-tract physics to a recognition task. They describe frequency regions favored by the air passage, so a pair of formant measurements gives a compact description of part of the vowel’s acoustic pattern. The proposed network uses those measurements as its input instead of receiving the entire sound waveform.

The recognition problem asks how that pattern should be mapped to a vowel category. The measurements describe the sound; the output labels describe the alternatives among which the model will choose. Learning this mapping would require relating the input patterns to the intended categories.

The stated goal is to train on students’ formant measurements. This establishes what information the model is meant to use and what it is meant to recognize. It describes a learning task, rather than supplying a completed test of how accurately the network recognizes the students’ vowels.

sections.title: A fully connected linear vowel network
teaching: The network begins with **F1 and F2**, two measurements of the sound. Each input has a particular meaning, so their order is part of the model’s definition. The network receives the formant pair rather than a speech waveform, and its job is to carry that information toward a choice among five labelled candidates.

A **fully connected layer** gives every receiving neuron a connection from every neuron in the preceding layer. Each connection has its own weight. The receiving neuron weights the incoming values and adds their contributions, allowing the same input pair to be combined differently by different neurons. One connection therefore has one weight; the neuron’s result depends on the combined incoming contributions.

The first hidden layer produces three internal values, which pass through layers producing two and then four values. These hidden values are intermediate combinations of the inputs. They are not additional formants measured from the sound or word labels already known to be correct. The result of one layer becomes the information available to the next.

The final five units correspond, from top to bottom, to /done/, /dune/, /dean/, /Don/, and /Dan/. Their order must stay attached to their labels when interpreting an output. A large value in a particular position is meaningful only when the associated candidate is known.

The architecture is **purely linear**: no activation function changes a weighted result between the displayed layers. Successive layers perform successive weighted combinations. This describes information flow, but a sequence of linear layers does not by itself turn the final values into a probability distribution.

sections.title: Random weights assign signed contributions to connections
teaching: A **weight** controls how an incoming value contributes to a receiving neuron. Each incoming value is scaled by its own connection weight, and the resulting contributions are added. The same F1 and F2 measurements can therefore produce different internal values when different neurons use different weights.

The sign and size of a weight have different roles. For a given incoming value, changing the sign reverses the direction of its contribution. Changing its magnitude changes how strongly that connection contributes. Positive and negative contributions can reinforce or oppose one another in the receiving neuron’s **weighted sum**, so one strong connection does not determine the result by itself.

The network begins with **randomly initialized weights**. Their displayed values describe a starting configuration of connections, rather than knowledge acquired from vowel examples. A random weight attached to an output labelled /dean/ is not evidence that the network has learned to recognize dean.

The distinction between an input and a parameter matters. The formant measurements describe the example currently being presented. The weights describe how the network processes that example and other examples. A forward pass uses the current weights to combine the inputs; learning would change the weights so that the combinations become more useful for the recognition task.

sections.title: Forward flow and an illustrative output distribution
teaching: A **forward pass** carries the current formant measurements through the network using its current weights. The first layer combines the inputs, the next layer combines those results, and the process continues to the five output units. This is **inference**, or producing an output with the model as it currently stands. Learning is different because it changes the weights used in that process.

The illustrated p(word) bars assign 0.5 to /done/, 0.2 to /Dan/, and 0.1 to each of the other three candidates. The largest bar expresses the strongest support in that distribution. The smaller bars preserve alternative possibilities instead of stating that every other candidate is impossible.

For values to represent probabilities across these alternatives, they must be nonnegative and add to one. The illustrated bars have those properties. The purely linear code, however, does not supply a rule that ensures them for its outputs. The probability bars illustrate the intended kind of categorical result; they are not a demonstrated calculation from the displayed random weights.

A predicted label and a **known target** also have different roles. The largest output indicates what the model favors. Deciding whether that choice is correct requires knowing which category the input example actually belongs to. The reaction symbol does not supply that target, so the favored candidate alone cannot establish a measured success or error.

sections.title: Declare the layer sequence in PyTorch
teaching: The PyTorch code turns the drawn layer sequence into a model definition. Importing torch makes the library available, and importing torch.nn as nn gives a shorter name for its neural-network building blocks. The variable net stores the sequence assembled from those blocks.

**nn.Sequential** specifies the order in which the layers pass their results onward. Each **nn.Linear** layer takes a fixed number of incoming values and produces a fixed number of outgoing weighted sums. Its first argument names the input width and its second names the output width. The output width of one layer matches the input width of the next so that the values can pass from stage to stage.

The sequence starts with the two formant inputs, passes through the three hidden layers, and ends with five candidate outputs. Each receiving unit has a separate weight for each incoming value. The declaration therefore expresses both which stages are connected and how many values each stage exchanges, without requiring a numerical calculation to understand the flow.

**bias=False** removes a separately added offset from the receiving units. It does not remove their connection weights or prevent those weights from changing during learning. With no activation functions inserted between the Linear layers, the displayed sequence remains purely linear.

Defining the architecture establishes how values will be processed. Running a formant example through it would be a forward pass, while learning would require examples and a procedure that changes the weights. The supplied declaration stops at defining the model, so it does not itself demonstrate a trained recognizer or compute the illustrated probability bars.
